item.title: Surviving the Split-Brain (Distributed Consensus)
item.description:
1. Problem Statement & Scope

A student confidently explains that they have built a Highly Available (HA) database by deploying two master nodes. If Master A goes down, a load balancer automatically routes all traffic to Master B. They tell you they have achieved 100% uptime.

You pull the literal plug on the network switch connecting Data Center A to Data Center B. Both masters are still powered on, but they cannot talk to each other. Because they cannot see each other, both assume the other is dead. Both promote themselves to the primary writer. For three hours, Master A accepts writes from European clients, while Master B accepts writes from Asian clients.

item.title: The Living Map (Dynamic Pathfinding & Telemetry)
item.description:
1. Problem Statement & Scope

Building a static mapping application is a solved computer science problem. You load a graph into memory and run A* Search. However, building a living map—one that ingests continuous telemetry from millions of moving vehicles to dynamically adjust edge weights and recalculate active routes in real-time—is a monumental exercise in stream processing, parallel computing, and advanced graph theory.

Functional Requirements

  • Spatial Resolution: Map raw GPS coordinates (latitude/longitude) to the nearest logical road segment.
  • Dynamic Pathfinding: Calculate the optimal route between two points based on current traffic conditions, not just static speed limits.
  • Active Re-routing: Continuously monitor active trips and proactively push new routes to clients if a faster path emerges due to sudden congestion.

Non-Functional Requirements

  • Massive Write Ingestion: The system must swallow millions of GPS telemetry pings per second without bottlenecking.
  • Sub-Second Latency: Route calculation must complete in $< 100$ms, even for cross-country queries.
  • Eventual Consistency for Traffic: A sudden highway closure should reflect in the routing engine’s weights within seconds.

2. Back-of-the-Envelope Estimation

  • Active Users: 10 million concurrent drivers actively navigating.
  • Telemetry Ingestion: Each client pings their GPS location every 5 seconds.
    • $10,000,000 / 5 = 2,000,000$ write QPS.
  • Routing Requests: Most users just drive; they only request a full route calculation at the start of a trip or upon missing a turn. Assume 20,000 QPS for pathfinding.
  • Graph Size in RAM: The entire road network of a large country (e.g., India or the US) contains tens of millions of nodes (intersections) and edges (road segments). Storing this graph with basic metadata (speed limits, segment IDs) requires roughly 20GB to 50GB of RAM. This easily fits into the memory of a single modern server, meaning the graph can be highly replicated rather than sharded.

3. High-Level Design (HLD)

To handle the dichotomy between massive write-heavy telemetry and read-heavy graph traversal, we completely decouple the ingestion pipeline from the routing engine using a stream processing architecture.

item.title: The Semantic Chunking Engine (Advanced RAG)
item.description:
1. Problem Statement & Scope

A junior engineer comes to you complaining that their Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) application is hallucinating. They loaded 10,000 enterprise PDFs into a vector database, but when they ask the LLM a question, it returns garbled nonsense.

You look at their ingestion script and see they are using a naive text splitter: rigidly cutting the text every 500 tokens. They have sliced sentences in half, separated Python function definitions from their return statements, and completely obliterated the structural hierarchy of financial tables.

item.title: The Autonomous Research Agent (LangChain Tool Architecture)
item.description:
1. Problem Statement & Scope

A graduate student presents a project to you. They are tired of manually hunting for papers, so they want to automate their weekly academic literature surveys and trend analysis across journals and conferences.

They propose building a LangChain-based autonomous agent. They want to give a Large Language Model (LLM) a set of custom tools—allowing it to query the IEEE API, scrape arXiv, download PDFs, extract the text, and synthesize a comprehensive markdown report of the latest trends in distributed systems.

item.title: Flash Sale & Ticketing Platform (Ticketmaster)
item.description:
1. Problem Statement & Scope

Designing a ticketing platform for a massive stadium tour is one of the most uniquely hostile environments in software engineering. Unlike a standard e-commerce platform where inventory gradually depletes over weeks, a highly anticipated concert triggers an instantaneous, deliberate Denial of Service (DoS) attack from your own legitimate customers. Two million humans and millions of automated scalper bots will hit your servers at exactly 10:00:00 AM.

item.title: The Indestructible Payment Gateway
item.description:
1. Problem Statement & Scope

Building a payment gateway is fundamentally different from building a social network. If a tweet drops, nobody cares; if a user is double-charged for a massive block of Nifty 500 stocks during an IPO allotment, you face catastrophic financial and legal ruin. The engineering focus shifts entirely from eventual consistency and raw throughput to absolute, immutable correctness.

Functional Requirements

  • Payment Execution: Process credit cards, net banking, and UPI transactions securely.
  • Idempotency: Guarantee that a duplicated request across a flaky network never results in a double charge.
  • Asynchronous Webhooks: Notify merchants reliably when a transaction clears, fails, or is refunded.

Non-Functional Requirements

  • Strict ACID Compliance: Financial ledgers cannot tolerate race conditions or lost updates.
  • Immutability: Data can never be UPDATED or DELETED. Errors are corrected via compensating transactions (append-only).
  • High Availability: The gateway must continue accepting payment intents even if downstream banking networks are experiencing downtime.

2. Back-of-the-Envelope Estimation

  • Throughput: 10,000 Transactions Per Second (TPS) peak.
  • Payload Size: ~2KB per transaction record (including metadata, cryptographic signatures, and routing info).
  • Storage: 10,000 TPS $\times$ 2KB $\times$ 86,400 seconds = ~1.7 TB/day. Over a year, this is roughly 600 TB. We will need cold-storage archiving for auditing, but hot storage must be exceptionally fast.
  • Latency: The gateway must respond to the client in $< 200$ms, even if the actual bank settlement takes days.

3. High-Level Design (HLD)

4. Deep Dive: Component Design

The Idempotency Layer

A mobile client sits on a train edge network. They click “Buy”. The request reaches the server, the database commits the transaction, and the server replies HTTP 200 OK. However, the train goes through a tunnel, and the client never receives the response. The client reconnects and retries the exact same request. How do you prevent charging them twice?
